title: Stanford NLP Group (@stanfordnlp)
summary:
This aligns with our internal audit findings: benchmarks without stakeholder input create false confidence. OpenEval’s participatory design could be a model for enterprise compliance workflows.
Quoting @stanfordnlp
For this week's NLP seminar, we are excited to host @ZiangXiao from Johns Hopkins University!
Date and Time: Thursday, May 21, 11:00AM — 12:00 PM Pacific Time.
Zoom Link:
Title: Evaluation is Power. How can we use it well?
Abstract: Evaluation steers the field of AI. It shapes what is worth building, what counts as progress, and what gets deployed and regulated. However, are our evaluation practices keeping pace with that responsibility? Benchmarks often fail to measure what they claim, and practitioners rarely find that these evaluations translate into actionable improvements. In this talk, I argue that good AI evaluation rests on two foundations. First, validity. Drawing on measurement science, we developed a conceptual framework with tools that treat benchmark design as the disciplined construction of measurement instruments. This approach exposes hidden assumptions and makes evaluation accountable to the constructs it intends to capture. Second, human-centeredness. A methodologically rigorous evaluation can widen the sociotechnical gap if the construct was chosen without the people it concerns. I show how HCI methods can help us reveal frictions in human-AI interaction that benchmarks often overlook. I will close by introducing OpenEval, an ongoing infrastructure effort to realize these two foundations, and show how it enables more valid, auditable, and participatory evaluation. Evaluation is power. We should use it well.
Hope to see you all there!

One of my favorite lectures I've watched this year is Stanford's CS336 lecture 7 on GPU parallelism.
It builds up the foundations by teaching the fundamental operations like broadcasting, scattering, gathering, reducing, all-gathering and all-to-all from first principles and gives you an intuition for how these connect to the multi GPU setup in part 1 of the lecture.

The reason why I love the teaching methodology of this particular lecture is that it goes into the practical details right away and hands you the code for what this conceptually would look like if you were to see it in a codebase.

The Stanford NLP Group questions whether there will be an AI jobpocalypse. Their view varies depending on mood and recent conversations, noting that no one in tech has clear insight into future employment trends. Economists are also uncertain.

A quoted report from @danshipper explains that despite automating many tasks with AI agents, the number of human workers has increased from 4 to 30 since GPT-3. The arXiv paper provides a detailed analysis of this phenomenon, emphasizing its implications for designing and interpreting human-AI workflows.

title: Stanford NLP Group (@stanfordnlp)
summary:
For the last NLP seminar of the quarter, we are excited to host @GretaTuckute from Harvard University!
Date and Time: Thursday, May 28, 11:00AM — 12:00 PM Pacific Time.
Zoom Link:
Title: Learning and Representing Language in Brains and LLMs
Abstract: For the first time in history, we have a system other than the human brain that can generate fluent language: large language models (LLMs). Do the human brain and LLMs converge on shared representations and computations, and if so, what can LLMs tell us about the nature of human linguistic representations? In this talk, I will first characterize the human language network, a set of frontal and temporal brain regions that causally support language processing. I will then show that the alignment between the human language network and LLMs is strong enough that LLMs can non-invasively modulate language responses in the human brain. Moreover, this alignment can be attributed to small sets of interpretable LLM-based features, providing insight into the main axes of brain activity when humans comprehend sentences. Finally, I will turn to the question of how such linguistic representations can emerge from the messy acoustic signals that humans actually receive. I will introduce AuriStream, a self-supervised textless NLP model that learns from continuous speech and shows that linguistic structure can emerge without prespecified text tokens, given the right temporal predictive learning objective. Together, these results position LLMs as tools for characterizing the representational principles in the human language network—and AuriStream as a step toward understanding which inductive biases can give rise to human-like language representations from raw speech.
Hope to see you all there!

Very excited for this discussion. Quoting @stanfordnlp: For the last NLP seminar of the quarter, we are hosting @GretaTuckute from Harvard University.

The talk explores whether large language models (LLMs) and the human brain share representations and computations in language processing. It characterizes the human language network in the brain and shows that LLMs can non-invasively modulate language responses in humans, thanks to strong alignment between the two. This alignment is linked to interpretable LLM features that reveal main axes of brain activity during sentence comprehension.

The speaker also introduces AuriStream, a self-supervised, textless NLP model trained on continuous speech, demonstrating that linguistic structure can emerge from raw acoustic signals without predefined text tokens. These findings suggest LLMs can serve as tools to understand human language representations, and AuriStream offers insights into how language might develop from raw speech.

summary:
Another on my to-read list... Especially if Jurafsky is involved.
Quoting @rohanpaul_ai
AI can make people feel more efficient even when they are not actually becoming much more efficient.
New paper from MIT, Stanford, New York Univ, Princeton.
That people often use AI for simple tasks because it feels like it saves time and effort, but the measured benefit is often tiny, missing, or even negative.
The biggest point is the feedback loop: once people use AI, they become more likely to use it again, even for easy tasks where doing it themselves would often be just as fast or faster.
i.e. AI dependence can grow from a mistaken feeling of convenience, not just from real productivity gains.
Across three preregistered studies with 2,691 participants, people used AI for basic arithmetic, spelling, recall, and short rewriting at higher rates than they predicted, especially on easy tasks.
They also expected AI to save 55.7 seconds on average, when the measured saving was only 7.5 seconds.
For simple work, the hidden cost is not intelligence but interface friction: writing the prompt, waiting, reading, checking, and deciding whether the answer is acceptable.
Once that loop begins, it can feel like effort has been outsourced, even when effort has only been rearranged.
Here’s the key part: the study suggests that AI use can train its own justification.
After using AI on just two tasks, participants became more likely to use it again, even when independent completion was faster.
The danger is not dramatic dependence, but quiet recalibration.
A person who asks AI for a trivial answer today may not become less capable tomorrow, but they may become less accurate at judging when their own mind is already the faster tool.
----
arxiv. org/abs/2605.22687
"The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks"

summary:
I love attending conferences focused on research, and @CAISconf this week was great! Hearing what's happening on the bleeding edge is fascinating. Yesterday @percyliang gave a great talk on training open frontier models with modest compute, and doing it as real science.
A few takeaways:
accuracy = algorithmic efficiency × resources. As a researcher you don't need the best model, you need to prove your efficiency is better. Algorithmic progress is real: LM efficiency has been halving compute every ~8 months.
The early Marin "YOLO runs" were a great look under the hood: annealing the LR and watching training loss creep up (fixed with z-loss), bad loss spikes the model never recovers from (added QK-norm), and a mysterious loss jump during cooldown that traced back to a bad RNG not shuffling data. More technical, but getting this inside look was super cool! Not exactly what you'll read in papers
The real shift: stop tuning individual runs, tune a scaling recipe. A recipe is a parametric mapping from compute to the full training config: given a compute budget, it tells you the number of params, tokens, learning rate, batch size, depth, etc. So instead of asking "what hyperparameters for this one model," you ask "what's the rule that picks hyperparameters at any scale." then fit your scaling laws on that. As Percy put it, "scaling laws don't happen automatically. You have to will them into existence."
Predictability is the bar for science: preregister the predicted loss on GitHub, then check it. They hit it within ~0.005 loss at 300x the FLOPs they fit on - same story on the MoE, within ~0.02, no spikes.
Open development > open weights. A real spectrum: closed (API-only) → open-weight (Llama, DeepSeek) → open-source (OLMo, Nemotron) → open development (Marin). Most "open" models just hand you weights. Marin/OpenAthena exposes the whole process: weights, code, data recipe, and the live research itself, where anyone (or any agent) can submit an experiment like a PR to Linux.
An analogy I liked: AI today is where software was in 1999. Open source back then wasn't obviously going to win, but it became the foundation everything got built on. Percy's bet is that truly open models follow the same arc and become the default infra for research and business, and I hope he's right! We desperately need stronger open source (truly open source) models

clean_summary:
Offloading Score is a metric designed to measure how much AI relies on human input by analyzing counterfactual workflows. It assesses the extent to which AI systems depend on human intervention by examining alternative scenarios where human involvement is altered or removed.

The work introduces a method to quantify reliance on AI versus human effort, providing insights into the true autonomy of AI systems. Experiments on various tasks demonstrate how the Offloading Score can reveal the degree of AI dependence, which is important for understanding AI's capabilities and limitations.

clean_title: Stanford's free STORM tool for web-based research reports
summary:
Well, maybe the real point is that interesting new research and product directions get explored by us and other university research labs first!
🤔
Quoting @heynavtoor
Stanford built a free version of Deep Research a year before OpenAI and Perplexity launched theirs.
Six researchers at Stanford published it: Yijia Shao, Yucheng Jiang, Theodore Kanell, Peter Xu, Omar Khattab, and Professor Monica Lam.
The paper went up in February 2024. OpenAI launched their $200 a month Deep Research in February 2025. Perplexity launched theirs at $20 a month two weeks later.
The Stanford version was free the whole time.
It's called STORM. You type a topic. It searches the web, reads sources, and writes you a full report with citations.
Most AI tools answer your question by guessing what you want. STORM does something different. It looks at existing articles on similar topics, figures out what questions are missing, and asks itself follow-ups like a journalist interviewing an expert. The answers become the report.
What you get:
- A topic-to-report engine that cites every source
- A live web demo, no install needed
- A second version called Co-STORM that lets you join in and steer the research
- A mind map that grows as the AI learns
- Plug in any AI model you want, including local ones
Try it at No login. No subscription. Over 70,000 people already have.
28,292 stars on GitHub. 2,578 forks. MIT license, free for any use.
OpenAI charges $200 a month. Perplexity charges $20 a month. Stanford charges nothing, ships the source code, and has the peer-reviewed paper to back the work.
The paper is older than the paywall.
